items.quote: ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

These trends can be largely rationalized based on geometric arguments related to confinement. The negative trend with respect to the density feature can be explained by its inverse correlation with framework size. A larger density of sites in a zeolite usually corresponds to smaller pore sizes or reduced occupiable volume, which increases confinement and thereby reduces the fraction of retained entropy. We point the reader to Figure S11 for a heatmap of the feature correlation matrix. In contrast, the largest spherical diameter that can be included along a free path (lsd_p) and the largest free sphere (lsd_f) show positive trends between the Shapley value and their respective feature value. We emphasize that a small lsd_f or lsd_p does not exclusively guarantee a small entropy ratio; rather, a combination among the framework features is the best predictor. In particular, for frameworks with especially small lsd_f (<2 [Å]), we find that on average, more entropy is retained among the adsorbates than within larger lsd_f frameworks (consider Figure S12). This phenomenon suggests the presence of "ink bottle"-shaped pores, where the channels connecting the larger pores of the framework are smaller and entropically less favorable than the cages that precede them. items.quote: Nevertheless , linear relationships between the adsorbed and gas-phase entropies persist for acidic $ ^ { 25 } $ and siliceous frameworks , $ ^ { 10 } $ suggesting that geometric descriptors may be suitable in further developing empirical correlations . The ideal gas entropy can be rigorously derived using statistical mechanics and depends on the degrees of freedom of the molecule. The greatest contributions to the gas-phase entropy are typically from the translational and rotational modes, which under isothermal conditions primarily depend on the system volume and principle moments of inertia of the molecule, respectively. Considering that adsorption limits the accessible volume and potentially hinders the rotational freedom of a molecule, it is conceivable that the entropy of adsorption may be predicted by using geometric arguments. For example, Denayer et al. have demonstrated that the driving force behind the zeolitic separation of alkane/isoalkane mixtures is exclusively the difference in rotational loss, represented by a ratio between the molecule's radius of gyration and the cavity's largest inscribed van der Waals radius. $ ^{26} $ De Moor et al. $ ^{27} $ used ab initio simulations to show that the adsorption entropies for n-alkanes within acidic zeolites are linearly correlated with their carbon number. Janda et al. $ ^{28} $ have studied the topological effects of protonic zeolites on the thermodynamics of n-alkane adsorption using Monte Carlo simulations. The conclusions of their work showed that for unidimensional zeolites without cages, the ratio of the minimum to maximum channel diameters positively correlate with the entropy and enthalpy of adsorption. In particular, the enthalpy and entropy of adsorption become less negative for adsorption within channels which are oval shaped and are most negative for circular-shaped channels. They showed that the presence/absence of framework cages also impacts the thermodynamics of adsorption, suggesting that the alkanes exhibit more rotational freedom in cages vs channels. Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman $ ^{25} $ compiled experimentally determined adsorption entropies for alkanes adsorbed in nine aluminosilicate zeolites. They showed that the entropic loss upon adsorption could be linearly correlated with the molecule's gas-phase translational and rotational entropies and that the occupiable volume of a zeolite is a “universal” descriptor in predicting such losses. In a separate study, $ ^{10} $ we have qualitatively reproduced the trends found in Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman's work for a larger set of molecules within pure-silica zeolites using Monte Carlo calculations of the adsorption entropy at infinitely dilute conditions. In general, these works suggest that the adsorbate characteristics are relatively unimportant and support the perception that models based primarily on adsorbent characteristics may be an effective tool trends found in Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman ' s work for a larger set of molecules within pure-silica zeolites using Monte Carlo calculations of the adsorption entropy at infinitely dilute conditions . Two parameters were evaluated: the chemical shift difference ( $ \Delta\delta $) between the solid-state and liquid-state spectra and the spectral line width (fwhm) of each peak, which reflects line broadening due to molecular immobilization and local environmental heterogeneity within the zeolite framework. $ {}^{39-41} $ In this analysis, we specifically compared the $ \Delta\delta $ and fwhm values of methyl and methylene carbons because all three OSDAs contain similar methyl and methylene groups, which provides a consistent basis for direct comparison. Key criteria included molecular size and shape compatibility with the pore geometry as well as the presence of rigid structures such as aromatic rings. This work provides valuable insights into refining the a priori selection criteria for OSDAs, offering a systematic approach to enhance their design for targeted control of entropy effects in zeolite synthesis.

items.quote: The molecular weight is a fundamental physical quantity with a presence in the statistical mechanical expression of the translational entropy for an ideal gas, as well as in the hindered/free translator entropy approximation for adsorbates within protonic zeolites. $ ^{[11,13-16]} $ Likewise, the molecular weight is also related to the number of heavy atoms (non-hydrogen) of the molecule, which has been shown to linearly correlate with the adsorption entropy of alkanes within protonic zeolites. $ ^{[27]} $ Under standard conditions, the translational entropy is the most significant contribution toward the absolute entropy of a molecule and predictably experiences the most significant loss upon adsorption. The rotational moments of inertia make for excellent descriptors toward distinguishing among spherical, linear, and nonlinear adsorbates. Namely, molecules represented by a single sphere exhibit no rotational inertia, while linear and nonlinear molecules rotate about two and three axes, respectively. Collectively, the principle moments provide additional information about the shape of the molecule. For example, the ratio of the principle moments (i.e., $ I_1/I_3 $ and $ I_2/I_3 $) describes the molecule as being “rod-like”, “sphere-like”, “disc-like”, or “envelope-like”.⁵¹,⁵² More complicated expressions can also be derived and presumably learned by a NN model, such as the “molecular eccentricity”,⁵³ “inertial shape factor”,⁵² and “sphericity index”,⁵⁴ each of which provide additional information about the shape of the molecule. The rotational freedom of a molecule is generally the second largest contributor to the standard ideal-gas entropy of the adsorbate, and the principle moments of inertia are explicitly present in the rotational entropy equation. The principle moments are also found within the hindered/free rotor approximation for alkanes within protonic zeolites and organic molecules on two-dimensional catalytic surfaces.¹¹,⁵⁵,⁵⁶

Linearity in the correlation of $ s_{ads}^{\infty} $ with $ s_{gas}^{0} $ is the key feature of the results in Figure 1, as it corresponds to qualitatively similar observations in the entropy correlations disclosed in refs 13, 31, and 27. More importantly, though, our results show that the apparent linearity in the correlation of $ s_{ads}^{\infty} $ with $ s_{gas}^{0} $ persists for a larger set of chemically diverse adsorbates than was previously seen. As discussed in those references, such a simple correlation is an obvious opportunity for the development of an engineering correlation that allows for prediction of the adsorption entropy from a limited set of measurements (whether experimentally or computationally derived). Furthermore, we aim to build on the conclusions in refs 13, 31, and 27 by examining our own data in light of the physical arguments presented previously. As a brief review, the apparent linearity in adsorption entropy correlations derives from fundamental physical considerations. In ref 27, where their linear trend in the entropy correlations was approximately two-third, the authors offered a simplified explanation that the linear trend reflected a loss of approximately one-third of the translational and rotational entropies owing to adsorption. Dauenhauer and Abdelrahman $ ^{13} $ extended this argument to acidic zeolites by considering an additional loss of rotational entropy dependent on the adsorbate size and the pore volume. (Pure linear correlation of $ s_{ads}^{\infty} $ with $ s_{gas}^{0} $ is broken by the arguments in ref 13, but a visual linear correlation persists. We return to this point later in our work.) In this context, here, we develop data-driven thermodynamic models to predict entropy of adsorption ( $ \Delta S_{ads} $), isosteric heat ( $ Q_{st} $), and Henry's adsorption constant ( $ K_{H} $) from molecular and zeolite structural information. To train these models, we build on our previous work $ ^{10} $ to compute these thermodynamic quantities for an expanded set of 3690 molecule–zeolite system combinations covering 84 molecules (spanning 15 chemical categories) and 96 pure-silica zeolite frameworks. Such a large and diverse combination of molecules and zeolites has not been considered before and enables us to build robust predictive models and gain new physical insights. Specifically, our results show that adsorbed and gas-phase entropies are linearly correlated; however, the slope of this correlation has a nonlinear relationship with framework metrics (e.g., occupiable volume and limiting pore diameter). On the other hand, a feed-forward neural network (NN) model built on a set of simple geometric descriptors of the adsorbate and the zeolite can accurately capture this nonlinearity and predict all three thermodynamic quantities. Further, to understand which molecular and zeolite descriptors contribute most to adsorption properties, i.e., to explain the NN, we leveraged a game-theoretic concept, viz., Shapley values, to deconvolute and quantify the contribution of each descriptor to the model prediction. items.quote: With the use of GCMC calculations, we have calculated the Henry constants, Gibbs free energies of adsorption, adsorption enthalpies, and entropies for previously identified reaction intermediates in the tri/tetramerization reaction of ethylene in five different zeolitic frameworks where the pore diameter roughly ranges from 10.1 to 15.4 Å. Linear correlations are observed between the adsorption enthalpy and the molecular volume of the inserted guest molecule and between the adsorption entropy and the molecular volume of the guest molecule. The slopes $ a_{H,j} $ and $ a_{S,j} $ are host-dependent and are found to decrease as the pore size of the host structure increases. Moreover, since $ \Delta H_{ads} $ and $ \Delta S_{ads} $ appear linearly correlated, a confinement compensation temperature ( $ a_j $) can be defined. If reactions were run at this temperature in the microporous structure, the beneficial enhancement of adsorption enthalpies would be exactly canceled out by the loss in entropy. We have found that the confinement compensation temperatures decrease with increasing pore sizes from 5200 K ± 800 K for mazzite to 1500 K ± 150 K for VFI, but they remain much higher than the usual operating temperatures in catalysis. With the use of $ a_{H,j} $ and the confinement compensation temperature, reaction selectivities and activities can be calculated. The selectivity in $ \alpha $-octene formation increases with increasing $ a_{H,j} $ values; however, when the pore size becomes too small, as in mazzite, the key transition state structure to form $ \alpha $-octene cannot enter anymore, since its molecular volume is too large with respect to available volume of the host. Additionally, it is concluded that $ \alpha $-octene and $ \alpha $-decene selectivities are negatively impacted by an increase in temperature.
